newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia called to cut PNG aid over mercenaries.
newsitem.headline: Australia called to cut PNG aid over mercenaries.

text.p: Australia's Labor opposition called on the government on Friday to cut aid to Papua New Guinea after its northern neighbour stood firm on sending mercenaries into secessionist-wracked Bougainville island.

Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan on Thursday declared that mercenaries would be sent to Bougainville as advisors, rejecting demands by Australian Prime Minister John Howard that the plan be scrapped.
Australia's opposition foreign affairs spokesman Laurie Brereton said Howard should suspend defence cooperation and cut aid at least to the value of the money paid to the mercenaries.
"Prime Minister Chan's dismissal of the Howard government's representations is an affront to all Australians," Brereton said in a statement.

"The Howard government must now deliver this message through concrete measures which leave Sir Julius Chan in absolutely no doubt of what is at risk as a consequence of the introduction of hired assassins into our region," he said.

Chan has said the mercenary plan would cost A$36 million (US$28 million), the bulk of which would be spent on equipment such as helicopters. Australia gives Papua New Guinea A$320 million a year in various aid programmes.
The Bougainville Revolutionary Army has waged a nine-year secessionist rebellion in which thousands of people have died.

Chan said on Thursday the 40 mercenaries, hired by the British-based military consultancy Sandline International, would continue training troops and would be sent to Bougainville as advisors once the mission against rebels is launched.

"Not only do we have a contract, we've paid for the contract," Chan said in Port Moresby. "And not only that, they (the mercenaries) are on the ground and they are performing to the conditions of our contract."
But Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer told reporters in Perth on Friday that a negotiated resolution to the Bougainville conflict was still possible.
"I believe it is possible, with patience and hard work, to achieve a political and peaceful solution to the problem in Bougainville," Downer said.
